title: Your product doesn't need an ad. It needs a format.
dek: What a famous curry taught me about creators with no budget, and a checklist for finding your own format.

cover.alt: Brick Lane Curry House case by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil: 1.47M views on one phaal reel, with zero paid creators
cover.cap: From the [Brick Lane Curry House case study](/work/brick-lane-phaal/).

body: Brick Lane Curry House has a dish with a reputation. Its phaal is the curry Adam Richman took on in [Man v. Food](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_v._Food) in 2009, the one Hot Ones host Sean Evans fed to Rhett & Link in a [2017 special at the restaurant](https://thetvdb.com/series/hot-ones/episodes/6050164), and one [Time Out](https://timeout.com/newyork/restaurants/spiciest-dishes-in-nyc) still lists among the spiciest dishes in New York. People walk in asking for it by name. That's the kind of story most brands would pay for. What the restaurant didn't have was a budget for paid creators.
So we stopped treating the phaal like a menu item and started treating it like a format.
**An ad** asks for attention once. **A format** earns it every week, because people know the shape and want to see who's next.
**The phaal challenge** already had a villain, a stake and a reaction, so we ran it as a recurring show on the restaurant's own channels.
**Creators came in as contestants,** not paid billboards. One collaboration reached 1.47 million views with no paid creators.
**Your format** is probably the thing customers already repeat about you without being asked.

The phaal started as the least interesting dish on the menu. Chef Satinder Sharma, who opened Brick Lane on East 6th Street in 2002, decided that if he was going to make something spicy, he'd do it justice. Habaneros first, then Scotch bonnets, bhut jolokia and the [Carolina Reaper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolina_Reaper), bought straight from [Ed Currie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Currie), the grower who bred it. The Reaper held the Guinness record for the world's hottest chili for a decade.

When Man v. Food showed up, the dish "snowballed into something so big, unintentionally," he told me. He calls it the infamous phaal who made them famous. A story like that is already doing the work an ad would do. It just needs somewhere to happen every week.
A challenge is already a show

Look at what the phaal challenge already has: a known villain, a clear stake and a reaction at the end. That isn't an ad. It's a show that can run every week. Formats are what bring people back, because the audience knows the shape and wants to see who's next.

So we turned the challenge into a recurring content property on the restaurant's own channels. One phaal reel, a collaboration with [First We Feast](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DDfpOyOvk33/), reached 1.47 million views.
The best format in food is a challenge

Look at the most famous food show on YouTube. [Hot Ones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Ones), made by First We Feast since 2015, is one setup repeated hundreds of times: ten wings, each hotter than the last, and a celebrity answering questions while they burn. The guest changes every week. The shape never does. When Ed Currie unveiled Pepper X, the pepper that took the Reaper's record, he did it [on Hot Ones](https://www.npr.org/2023/10/17/1206450553/worlds-hottest-pepper-guinness-record-pepper-x).

That's the audience the phaal belongs to. So when our reel went out as a collaboration with First We Feast, it didn't land in their feed as an ad. It looked like the next episode of something they already watch.

A format also fixes the budget problem. If the phaal is a show, creators aren't people you pay to hold your food up to the camera. They're contestants, and they want the content as much as the restaurant wants the reach.

I pitched more than ten food creators myself, DMs and all, on a zero-budget creator strategy. We brought in Priya's Plates as our guest and posted [her attempt](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DBWjEWBvpIV/) as a collaboration, so it reached both audiences at once. It passed 58,000 views with nearly 300 shares.

Most brands already have one and walk past it. Look for the thing customers repeat about you without being asked: the dish people dare each other to order, the question every new client asks, the ritual your regulars have.

Then give it a shape that repeats. The same setup, the same stakes, a new face every time. Run it on your own channels so you own it, and invite creators in as guests so their audiences meet you inside a story instead of an ad break.
**A known hero or villain.** The phaal, the hardest question, the impossible build.
**A clear stake.** Finish it or don't. Get it right or don't.
**A reaction at the end.** The payoff people wait for and send to a friend.
**A new face every time.** Guests keep it fresh, and the shape keeps it familiar.
**A home you own.** Post on your own channels and as a collaboration, so every guest's audience lands on yours.
Paying creators to hold the product up to the camera.
Changing the shape every week, so nobody learns what to expect.
Letting the guest post alone. A collaboration post reaches both audiences at once.
Hiding the backstory. The story behind the product is the hook.
If your product has a famous story, it doesn't need an ad. It needs a format.
**What is a content format?** A repeatable setup with the same shape every time, such as a challenge, a series or a ritual, where only the guest or the subject changes.

**Can a restaurant grow on social media without paying creators?** Yes, if it gives creators something they want to make. Brick Lane's phaal challenge reached 1.47 million views on one reel with zero paid creators.
**What is phaal?** A curry built to be as hot as possible. Brick Lane's is made with some of the world's hottest peppers and became famous through Man v. Food.
The full story, with the numbers and the chef in his own words, is in the [Brick Lane Curry House case study](/work/brick-lane-phaal/).
